headline.method_note: Tonnage-weighted average of scenario_A_pct (or scenario_B_pct) across food groups with a resolved numeric self-sufficiency figure, weighted by each group's Scenario A recommended-demand tonnage. Excludes groups with no single point estimate (legumes, porridges/pasta/rice/grain products, sweets & discretionary) -- coverage_pct_of_tonnage states what share of total national food-group demand this average actually represents, so the headline number is never presented as more complete than it is. A further 3 items (legumes, and the two near-zero individual oil types) have no Scenario A demand tonnage available at all and so cannot even be excluded-with-visibility -- they simply carry no weight in this calculation; legumes in particular is a genuine, separately-flagged gap. Scenario C (EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet) uses the same weighting basis and the same exclusion logic -- see scenario_C_excluded_from_average for its own list, which differs slightly from A/B because EAT-Lancet leaves a different subset of categories unresolved. Scenario C.2 (the 2025 EAT-Lancet Commission's revised Planetary Health Diet, Phase 14) uses the same weighting basis and exclusion logic again -- see scenario_C2_excluded_from_average.

food_groups.note: Phase 12 update: FAOSTAT 2022 filled the oats gap (238.1% self-sufficient, previously blank) and gave real human-food consumption weights (kg/capita/yr: rice 4.77, barley 7.78, oats 5.97) to split this RTU011 category by consumption share -- rice 25.8%, oats+barley 'porridge grains' 74.2% -- the same per-capita-share splitting technique already used for the RTU011 poultry/red-meat split (Phase 3). Weighted blend of just those two parts: ~156.2%, presented as an UPPER BOUND (not the resolved category figure) because pasta (durum wheat, ~0% self-sufficient per PM20's 0% durum production) is still excluded for lack of a consumption weight -- FAOSTAT doesn't separate durum from bread wheat. Since pasta is very likely near 0% too, folding it in could only pull the true figure down, never above this bound. Narrowed from the prior 0%-178%+ span (128 points wide, effectively uninformative) to a single-sided 156.2% ceiling with a stated, real weighting behind it. See PHASE12_NOTES.md. Phase 13 verification: the user correctly pointed out Estonia produces pasta domestically (Tartu Mill) and grows its own wheat -- confirmed true (Tartu Mill's own product listing gives spaghetti ingredients as durum wheat flour and water; Wikipedia confirms Tartu Mill mills wheat/rye flour, semolina, pasta and feed). But the wheat Estonia grows in large surplus is common/soft wheat (bread and feed wheat), not the durum wheat pasta requires -- per PIKK.ee's agricultural extension guide, 'Estonia grows soft wheat varieties because durum needs a drier, more continental climate' than Estonia has, and per ERR/Novaator (2024), durum is only being trialled experimentally by a single farm (Põlgaste, two growing seasons as of the article), explicitly framed as an uncertain experiment dependent on finding a buyer -- not a tracked commercial crop. So pasta-MAKING is genuinely domestic (confirms the user's point), but it runs on imported durum wheat/semolina, the same way a country can roast imported coffee or process imported cocoa domestically without being self-sufficient in the raw crop. This replaces the earlier, unverified per-PM20 0%-durum-production claim (PM20 does not track durum separately) with sourced confirmation that pasta's raw-material self-sufficiency really is ~0%, so 156.2% remains a valid upper bound. See PHASE13_NOTES.md. Phase 14: Scenario C.2 (2025 EAT-Lancet, whole grains 210g/day vs 232g/day in 2019) demand computed and added as a ratio column; self-sufficiency stays unresolved for the same reason as Scenario C (no resolved Scenario A point estimate to scale).
food_groups.flag_reason: Phase 12 narrowed this from an unresolved 0%-178%+ span to a ~156.2% upper bound (rice 0% + porridge grains 210.4%, FAOSTAT-weighted; pasta still excluded, unweighted) -- still not a single resolved point estimate, so still flagged as a data gap, but a substantially tighter one. Phase 13 confirmed (rather than assumed) that pasta's raw material, durum wheat, is not commercially grown in Estonia (soft wheat only, per PIKK.ee; durum is experimental-only per ERR/Novaator 2024) even though pasta is manufactured domestically at Tartu Mill from imported durum. See PHASE12_NOTES.md and PHASE13_NOTES.md.

food_groups.note: Statistikaamet's PM29 honey balance (production 1,313 t, human consumption 1,339 t, 2024) sat unused in data/raw/statistikaamet/ since Phase 1 -- wired in for the first time in Phase 12. TAI's Table 13 doesn't give honey its own recommended-portion count (it's only one of five equally-weighted items in Table 16's representative sweets gram-weight), so Scenario B/C honey demand is extrapolated using the whole 'Sweets, snacks & discretionary (total)' category's own demand-change ratios (0.323x for B, 0.1743x for C) -- an explicit assumption that honey's consumption share moves proportionally with the rest of sweets, not a TAI-specific honey figure. Production held fixed (no capacity-ceiling modelling, consistent with every other subitem). Net effect: moving toward recommended (lower) sweets consumption leaves Estonia even MORE comfortably honey-self-sufficient (>300% under Scenario B), since less consumption against fixed production only helps. See PHASE12_NOTES.md. Phase 14: Scenario C.2 (2025 EAT-Lancet) cuts added sugar far more sharply than the 2019 diet did (6g/day vs 31g/day), so the same proportional-extrapolation method used for B/C pushes honey's C.2 self-sufficiency to a striking ~2,795% -- not because honey production changes, but because the 2025 diet's much smaller sugar allowance shrinks the denominator dramatically. Read this as 'a diet that ate that little sugar would find Estonia's existing honey production trivially sufficient for its entire (much smaller) sweets allowance,' not as a claim about honey specifically improving.
food_groups.flag_reason: Well above every self-sufficiency threshold in every scenario; production is fixed and recommended (lower) sweets consumption only strengthens this further. No critical dependency. Phase 12 addition; see PHASE12_NOTES.md.

faostat_cross_check.note: Close match: FAOSTAT 2022 raw wheat+rye ratio (322%) lands within ~3 percentage points of the PM20-2024-derived bread proxy (332.5%), despite different years and different exact item scope (FAOSTAT tracks raw grain, not bread). Strengthens confidence in the yield-cancellation argument for grain specifically.

Same ballpark (205% FAOSTAT 2022 vs 178% PM20 2024) -- both comfortably >100%, supporting the qualitative point that barley is the strong end of the porridge/pasta/rice range, even though the range itself stays unresolved.
Close match: FAOSTAT 2022 (65.8%) sits almost exactly at the project's headline figure (66.9%, itself a midpoint of a 63.7% derived / 70% official split). Good independent confirmation.

MATERIAL DIVERGENCE, flagged not resolved: FAOSTAT 2022 shows just 9.2% -- well below both the project's derived (29%) and headline/official (46%) figures. Possible drivers: FAOSTAT's international commodity classification for 'Vegetables, Other' may be narrower than Statistikaamet's PM33 category; international reporting for minor-crop production in small countries can lag or under-count relative to the national statistics office's own figures; 2022 may also have been a weaker vegetable-production year than the years underlying the official 5-year average. This is the same vegetables/fruit gap already flagged as the project's largest unexplained divergence since Phase 1 -- FAOSTAT adds a THIRD data point that disagrees with both existing ones, rather than resolving the discrepancy. Treated as an open, documented uncertainty.

Close match: FAOSTAT 2022 fruit-only figure (6.5%) is close to the project's fruit+berries-combined 8% -- consistent given FAOSTAT's item list here doesn't appear to break out Estonia's wild/cultivated berries separately (a known FAOSTAT limitation for minor crops).

Notable divergence: FAOSTAT 2022 (75%) vs PM42 2024 (109%) -- different years for a sector (cattle) where herd size and slaughter volume can shift meaningfully year to year; possible carcass-weight or trade-accounting convention differences also plausible. Flagged, not resolved.
Reasonably close: FAOSTAT 2022 (78.2%) vs PM42 2024 (72%), within ~6 points.

Notable divergence: FAOSTAT 2022 (79.3%) is well above PM42 2024's headline (57.7%). Two years apart in a sector that has seen real investment/capacity changes in the Baltics is a plausible driver; a definitional difference in what counts as 'poultry meat' (broiler-only vs. incl. turkey/duck) is also possible. Flagged, not resolved -- this reinforces rather than undercuts Phase 6/7's caution in treating poultry's feed-adjusted and scenario-B figures as sensitivities, not precise points.
Close given small absolute volumes (a few kt either way swings the ratio a lot); not a meaningful precision test at this scale.
Close match: FAOSTAT 2022 (57.9%) within ~4 points of PM45 2024's headline (53.6%). Good independent confirmation.

Interesting: FAOSTAT 2022 (139.0%) lands almost exactly on the project's own DERIVED milk-equivalent figure (134.9%), not the official headline (166%). This is an independent data point supporting the derived bottom-up build over the official strategy-document figure for this category -- worth noting as it slightly shifts confidence relative to Phase 5's original 'prefer official when they diverge' default.

Near-exact match: FAOSTAT 2022 (303%) essentially confirms the official 300% resource-basis figure. Also independently corroborates the export-heavy caveat: FAOSTAT's own Food (human consumption) line for fish is 17kt against 88kt production -- ~19%, close to the ~15% 'stays domestic' figure already carried from Phase 2.

MATERIAL DIVERGENCE, flagged not resolved: FAOSTAT 2022 raw-rapeseed self-sufficiency is 141.3%, roughly double the PM37-2024-derived figure (69.3%) this project's oil estimate is built on. Two plausible, unconfirmed drivers: (1) 2022 was an unusual year for Baltic/Black Sea region oilseed trade following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which reshaped regional grain/oilseed flows -- a temporal effect, not necessarily a definitional one; (2) FAOSTAT's SUA/FBS accounting may treat seed crushed domestically for oil extraction differently from Statistikaamet's PM37 'domestic use' figure, particularly where the resulting oil is later exported. Not resolved -- presented as an open uncertainty.

CONFIRMS A FLAGGED LIMITATION: FAOSTAT 2022 refined-oil self-sufficiency is 265%, far above the 69.3% yield-cancellation proxy. Phase 5's own methodology note already flagged that the yield-cancellation argument 'breaks down if a meaningful share of Estonia's edible oil trade is in already-refined form rather than raw seed' -- this is exactly what FAOSTAT shows: Estonia produces far more refined rapeseed oil (61kt) than it consumes domestically (23kt supply), meaning a large share of crushed oil is exported directly as oil, not as raw seed. The true oil self-sufficiency is very likely well above the 69.3% raw-seed proxy, in Estonia's favour (i.e. the project's existing oils figure UNDERSTATES self-sufficiency, not overstates it) -- but the exact magnitude remains uncertain given the raw-seed-level divergence noted above.

Minor divergence, negligible in absolute terms: FAOSTAT shows a small 1kt of domestic sunflower-oil production/processing in 2022 vs. PM37 2024's 0t. Both indicate a near-total import dependency for this oil type regardless of the exact reading.
Exact match: both sources confirm 0% domestic rice production, consistent with the project's existing assumption.

CONFIRMS the existing assumption rather than revising it: FAOSTAT 2022 shows zero recorded tree-nut production against ~32kt domestic supply, i.e. exactly 0% -- Estonia's small-scale/garden hazelnut growing (real, per user feedback) doesn't register at national-statistics resolution. Phase 1's crosswalk had explicitly flagged this as needing a Phase 3 double-check against trade data that never happened until Phase 12; now confirmed rather than merely assumed.

Fills a genuine data gap rather than cross-checking an existing figure: the Phase 1 Statistikaamet PM20 pull had oats production blank for 2024 (not published that year), so this project had no oats self-sufficiency figure at all until this FAOSTAT pull. Adopted directly as the project's own oats figure (238.1%, even stronger than barley's 205.5%) in the absence of any Estonian-source alternative. See PHASE12_NOTES.md for how this was combined with barley and rice.
